blocks.text: We have already studied that a magnetic field is produced around a current-carrying conductor (Fig. 10.1). Also, a changing magnetic field gives rise to a current in a conductor placed in it. Electromagnetism is a key area of physics that studies how electric charges and magnetic fields interact.

blocks.title: Oersted, 1820
blocks.text: In 1820 Hans Christian Oersted (printed 'Orsted') found that electricity and magnetism are correlated: a current in a wire deflects a nearby compass needle, because the current produces a magnetic field around it.

Electromagnetism is crucial for modern technology, including phones, computers and medical devices. In this chapter we explore basic concepts like electric fields, magnetic forces and electromagnetic induction, and see how these principles affect both natural phenomena and technology. Understanding these concepts helps us appreciate how electromagnetism influences our world and drives innovation.

Magnetism started with lodestone, a natural mineral discovered in ancient Turkiye. Lodestone, or magnetite (Fe3O4), can attract metals like iron and steel and aligns with the Earth's magnetic poles, which led to the invention of the compass (For Your Information).

blocks.prompt: A current flows towards the north along a power line. In which direction is the magnetic field just above the wire (MCQ 10.1)?
blocks.explanation: By the right-hand grip rule, with the thumb pointing north along the current, the fingers curl so that just above the wire they point west. The answer is (d) west.

items: A current produces a magnetic field, and a changing magnetic field produces a current; electromagnetism studies how charges and magnetic fields interact. Oersted (1820) showed the link between electricity and magnetism.
Lodestone (magnetite, Fe3O4) from ancient Turkiye attracts iron and steel and led to the compass.
